utterances.text: If I -- if I could stop you there. When you say "contributions," could you identify for the Chamber what kind of contributions you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: We did not call them contributions but compensations. So it's maybe a matter of terminology. There was, for example, a special compensation for the conditions of life and work in a specific garrison or place where a person was assigned or where the unit where he was working was deployed. The conditions of work could be more difficult than somewhere else. Perhaps the unit was located outside of urban areas, so the conditions for performing his function were more difficult. There was the issue of his family, of educating the children, so then there were compensations. It was the same for compensation that was given for work that entailed special physical and mental efforts or if someone worked with dangerous chemicals or other dangerous materials, and so on. I cannot tell you all the details about the structure of the compensations, but the idea was that at specific posts that are not just the usual ones but which are in a way specific as compared to other duties that specific compensations would be received by such personnel. Not all the officers, but just those who perform such duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me interrupt and ask you this: It sounds like you're referring to a -- a compensation scheme that has a gross amount. I'm using the term "gross" meaning all of the component parts that could potentially go to any individual's, I'm going to call it salary for the moment, that may be the wrong term, but a gross amount that could be given to or allowed for any particular individual's performances. What was that called? Is there a name for that? How do you call that in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Yes, compensation for -- these compensations are set out in the rules on salaries. In these rules, all kinds of these compensations are specifically listed. I have forgotten what their names were. I don't know them all, but they are all spelled out precisely in these rules on salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: The officers who were assigned to such duties would then receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this -- this: Is the term "bruto plata" a definition of the gross salary?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Should I explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: The elements, which I listed, made up a salary. That was the salary which an officer would be paid. The basic salary, as we called it. And then certain contributions were also calculated and added to a salary. There were a number of these contributions, and the contributions were then paid to certain institutions, such as, for example, there was the contribution for pensions and invalid pensions. They were paid to the pension institutions. Then the contribution for health service was paid to the health care service, and specifically within the army, it was paid for the medical service within the army. In the civilian world it was paid to the civilian medical institutions. There was a whole scale of these contributions. The contribution for employment, for the communal needs, then for construction, land, and so on. I think there was about a dozen of these various contributions which were paid to the relevant institutions, and the state would then finance certain needs from these contributions. The majority of the contributions had a social character, a character of providing social care through the state. The citizens who were employed were entitled to have this kind of care or insurance. If it was old-age pensions it was paid to the social security fund of military personnel and so on. So the basic salary and the contributions together made the gross salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the contributions that you said had a social character, which body determined the amount of those social contributions? And by "body" I mean was that the Ministry of Defence, the parliament, the VJ. How did that occur? Who made those determinations, which organ?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: It was the federal government that did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the Defence budget itself, the budget that you helped prepare and plan, could you tell us, if you know in rough terms, what percentage of that budget was committed to or allocated for those -- that purpose, and the purpose I'm referring to is salaries and social contributions.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: It varied from one year to another. The budget always had to provide funds for salaries. That was a fixed category, as it were. That money simply had to be found. Now, the quota available that I spoke of this morning within which the army could move when planning the budget, whatever remained from these planned resources earmarked for salaries was then allocated for other purposes. Then the more money went -- the more money the defence budget received the higher the percentage was of salaries in the budget -- or, rather, it was the other way round. For example, when I came to head the administration, this percentage for personal incomes and pensions, because military pensions are paid out from the budget, it was, say, 45, 50, 55 per cent of the federal budget. However, from 1993 and in the years that followed, that percentage even reached 60 per cent, even 65 per cent of the total defence budget. Incredible but true. There were less and less resources in the budget and salaries had to be paid, so from that point of view, there were less possibilities for material equipment and for meeting other needs of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've heard various figures here in terms of what percentage of the defence budget was allocated for the VJ and what percentage of the defence budget was allocated for the Ministry of Defence. Could you give us, in your estimation, if you can, a breakdown in terms of the percentages that were allocated for those respective and independent units?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: There are two important points there. In the planning process, the ministry expressed its needs, and the Army of Yugoslavia expressed its needs. As for the needs of the ministry, well, the ministry did not have the army, and they did not have the same volume of spending as the army did. They were part of the state apparatus, and they had to pay for the regular way in which administration functioned. So these were small-scale resources. If we exclude military pensions, because that is a special category, we can say that, say, 5 to 6 per cent of these funds, taking into account salaries and other things that went to the Ministry, all the rest went to the army. However, when the budget was actually being implemented, the army was perhaps given 30 to 35 per cent of that budget because the Ministry of Defence paid out all salaries, and they made these major purposes for the army, especially combat equipment, complex equipment, especially from foreign countries, then buying different facilities and so on. The situation was a bit different. Well, plans did express the needs of the army. However, as far as the implementation was concerned, funds were kept at the level of the ministry. It was the minister who made a decision -- or, rather, his organs made decisions on these purchases, et cetera. Ultimately it was the ministry that used these resources and in this way met the needs of the army as planned. The funds did -- were actually earmarked for the General Staff, but it was all kept at the level of the ministry. So when I exclude military pensions from the military budget, 30 to 35 per cent was earmarked to the Army of Yugoslavia, and then the Army of Yugoslavia met -- or, rather, covered its current expenditures through that. That had to do with the regular life of the army. So it basically had to do with logistical support, food, clothing, daily requirements like in any household, if you will. Now we're looking at the army in a broader sense. Whatever is needed. Public utilities, electricity, heating, clothing, maintenance of buildings and the like. All of that was provided to the army. And then also the maintenance of technical equipment. The army was given money for those purpose, and that was 30 to 35 per cent, perhaps sometimes up to 40 per cent. But we never really looked at the percentages involved. However, that's the way you phrased your question. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, and that's because that's been the kinds of discussions we've been having here, and perhaps we've been phrasing the questions or the inquiry in an incorrect fashion. However, as I see the figures that you've just indicated, am I -- am I correct in my understanding that some -- something in the neighbourhood of over 50 per cent of the budget went to military pensions?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: No, not 50 per cent. Salaries and pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Salaries and pensions, about 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the distinction between salaries and pensions, are you in a position to give us any kind of breakdown as between salaries and pensions? If you are, that's fine, and if you aren't, that's understandable.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Well, I can. Out of the 60 per cent that has to do with salaries and pensions, we didn't actually make any calculations of that kind, but it's not hard to calculate it. When we say salaries, these were payments that were made at the level of the ministry in addition to the salaries. When we're talking about salaries, please take into account the fact that we always -- that we're always talking about gross salaries. That is to say, we include compensations, various benefits, say, given to officers who don't have apartments of their own, then also other compensations paid, say, for the reserve force, then payments made to the soldiers for training, education. We looked at all of that as personal expenditures. That is more than just pensions. So if we look at these personal payments, pensions included, perhaps it would be 15 to 20 per cent that went to pensions, and the rest remained in the hands of the ministry for those personal payments, as I referred to them. On the other hand, if we look at pensions in relation to the total budget where we have personal payments and material payments, pensions were, say, between 7 and 8 per cent of the total defence budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the disposition of any movable asset that had been used by the VJ, at the time that that asset was, for example, sold, where did those funds go? Did they go to the benefit of the VJ? Did they go back into the state coffers? Did they go to the MOD? Was there any mechanism for determining how the income that was realised from the sale of that asset would be distributed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: That question was regulated by the law on financing the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That law says that all income earned by the federal organs as they exercise their activities are paid into the federal budget and constitute one of the sources of the federal budget. However, part of these revenues, and I'm talking about the army now, I'm talking about the Ministry of Defence, remained in the ministry so that they could cover their costs that were incurred when earning that income, because there are certain costs involved when assets are being sold. It's a small portion. It was even prescribed, but the maximum amount involved was 20 per cent. The rest had to be paid into the federal budget. And later on within this total revenue of the federal budget, that went for the financing of federal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the issue of sanctions. As it related to the question of the budgets that were planned, did the sanctions themselves affect or require in any fashion a rebalancing of the budget, or did the budgets remain the same after the imposition of sanctions? And by budgets remaining the same, I mean the annual budgets.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two times, sometimes even three times. 1993 was a particularly characteristic year when unprecedented inflation was recorded in Yugoslavia, perhaps at a rate that had never been experienced in the world before. So then the budget had to be rebalanced. In 1994 and 1995 this was not done as often, perhaps once or twice. Then say in 1997 only once, but 1993 was different. Whenever it was concluded that the budget was insufficient for a particular federal organ, then the said organ would initiate proceedings with the federal government to increase the amount allocated for that organ. The government discusses the matter, but at any rate, it is the Federal Assembly that has to decide ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the -- that you've mentioned, the unprecedented inflation that was recorded in Yugoslavia, was -- if you know, was your monetary system pegged or tied to any hard currency system in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: In terms of calculations, what was always looked at was what it meant in terms of Deutschmark. So we looked at the nominal value of our dinar, and we measured it in relation to Deutschmark. Let me give an example for 1993, because that is when we had the biggest problem of all. In the beginning of 1993, the rate of exchange of the dinar vis-a-vis the Deutschmark, I cannot be very specific, I mean it was almost 20 years ago, well, 17 years ago. In the beginning of the year -- actually, it was in 1992 that inflation started rising abruptly. In the beginning of 1993 it was 50 dinars to a Deutschmark, to 1 Deutschmark. And at the end of the year it was almost 90 million dinars to 1 Deutschmark. Now, what percentage that might be -- if we were to express it in terms of percentage, what would that be? So you see how devalued it was. You see how high the rate of inflation was. It was very hard to view things. As a matter of fact, if we look at salaries, our salaries, if I received my salary in the morning it would be worth, say, 20 Deutschmark. By the evening of that very same day, it would fall to 10 or even 5 Deutschmark. It depended on how much foreign currency I could buy during the course of the day. There was this immense rise in inflation on a daily basis. Already in 1994 there was a monetary reform, so the ratio changed, one dinar to one Deutschmark. All of this was well prepared 1994 and 1995. That was the ratio, and there was a certain degree of stability in terms of the budget and in terms of life itself, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were referring to the issue of salaries, who was it that determined the rate of the salary, how high the salary would be? Would that be once again the federal government? Would that be the MOD? Would that be the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The federal government passed a decree on the salaries of military personnel and civilians serving in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue, as we've been discussing before, the issue of procurement of materials from abroad, when those materials were purchased, were those purchased, to your knowledge, in dinars, or were they purchased in foreign currency, what I would call for the moment hard currency?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: You couldn't buy anything with dinars in Holland or in any other country. You had to use the currency of the country that you were making your purchases in. Now, the Ministry of Defence obtained foreign exchange by buying some from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. They would give the counter-value in dinars to the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and the National Bank of Yugoslavia provided them with dinar -- with foreign exchange. There is a mechanism involved as to how these payments are made, and that is how we paid for these purchases abroad. We had a bank of our own which was called the Military Service attached to the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Later on it was called Jugarant Bank, and through this bank of ours, we bought foreign exchange from the National Bank of Yugoslavia and payments were made through that bank to a particular country where the purchase had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That what have occurred from the time that you -- that you became head of the finance department through your retirement, that you were in a position to obtain foreign currency for purposes of making foreign purchases or procurements abroad?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: That's right. Let me add one more thing, if you allow me to do so. If per chance the Army of Yugoslavia would earn some foreign currency, they had to deposit that foreign exchange with the National Bank of Yugoslavia. They could not use that money independently. I'm talking about the Ministry of Defence when I say "the army." It wasn't the General Staff that could do that, it was the Ministry of Defence. All foreign exchange had to be deposited with the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and when they needed foreign exchange then they would buy it from the national bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's always good to have younger and fresher minds about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanic, you've -- you told us at the beginning of your testimony that, I think, you were born in a region which was outside of Serbia. In fact, you were born in a region which would be considered Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you further told us that you were in Belgrade working for the Ministry of Defence during the period of time which was -- I'll call it the conflict period. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any orders to go back to the area where you'd been born?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: No. I was born in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but when I was 5 -- I was born in 1940, but in 1945, when I was 5 years old, after the Second World War, like other families from Bosanska Krajina, we moved to Banat, to Vojvodina. My father had been an officer, and after the Second World War, he was transferred to Nis, and it was there that I went to school, all the schools I attended before the military academy. I was a citizen of Serbia, so in military records or in state records I was not registered as a person from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So although I was born there, no one asked me or ordered me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the -- the rank that you held upon your -- your retirement, what rank was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: I retired as lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when were you first appointed a lieutenant general?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE JOVANIC
utterances.text: In 1999, the month of June 1999, because ranks were given on the occasion of holidays, and in June, on the 16th of June, there was a military holiday, and that's when military personnel would be promoted except for fast-track promotions. In 1993 I was made major general, so I was major general for years. And then in the year 2000, when I was 60 years old and after having had 40 years of active service, I received a military pension. I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and your testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note there is still some time left in the session, but I'm going to be longer than half an hour. I think I can reduce what's required if we can adjourn until tomorrow morning and if I could begin cross-examination tomorrow morning, Your Honours. I know there isn't another witness scheduled for tomorrow. I would comfortably complete cross-examination, I would expect, inside a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, I would -- I certainly would not object to that matter, because we're going to have to come back, I think, in any event tomorrow to discuss the issue that we had initially raised in private session. So it seems to make some kind of common sense to do it that way, and I certainly wouldn't wish to hurry Mr. Thomas in his examination. I'd like him to have the fullness of time to that which he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In that case, the court will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00, I believe in same court. Mr. Jovanic, you are bound until tomorrow by your oath taken today, and please do not discuss the case with any one of the parties. I hope you have a good rest today, and thank you very much for your testimony. Then the court adjourns until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
